subject: Automotive & EVs
title: The First Traffic Rules
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The First Traffic Rules.

hook.text: In the early 1900s, cars and horses shared roads with no lanes, signs, or rules.

buildup.text: Accidents were so common that some cities debated banning cars altogether.

discovery.text: William Phelps Eno designed the first stop sign and traffic circle for New York in 1903.

twist.text: Eno created modern traffic rules without ever learning how to drive a car himself.

climax.text: His one-way streets, crossings, and rotaries spread across the world within decades.

punchline.text: The father of traffic safety never drove a car.

quiz.question: What was unusual about traffic pioneer William Phelps Eno?

details.summary: The earliest traffic rules emerged in the early 1900s as growing car numbers created chaos, establishing speed limits, driving licenses, stop signs, and traffic lights for the first time.
details.whyItMatters: Without traffic rules, roads were deadly free-for-alls. The standardization of signs, signals, and licensing created the regulatory framework that makes modern mass motoring possible.
takeaways: Early speed limits were often just 10 to 15 miles per hour
The first electric traffic light appeared in Cleveland in 1914
Driver licensing began in the early 1900s in various countries

faq.question: When was the first stop sign installed?
faq.answer: The first stop sign appeared in Detroit, Michigan, in 1915. It was a simple black-and-white sign. The familiar red octagonal design was standardized much later in the 1950s across the United States.

faq.question: Were there traffic rules before cars existed?
faq.answer: Yes. Cities had rules for horse-drawn carriages, including speed restrictions and right-of-way conventions. However, the speed and volume of automobiles required a completely new framework of regulation.
